prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms enables measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep B012 with Katori and Ye as my single-part prize. I moved to it after the opening ballots, and the chair's summary rightly warns that convergence of eight members is not merit. So I re-tested the case on its own terms. The mechanism is specific: a lattice at the magic wavelength cancels the dominant light shift, and Lamb-Dicke confinement lets many neutral atoms be interrogated on an ultranarrow line without Doppler or recoil broadening. The performance is a measured quantity, about 1e-18 fractional uncertainty, and it has been reproduced in several laboratories and with Sr, Yb and Hg, which is the independent confirmation I would demand of any instrument result. The consequences are already in use in comparisons and constraints on fundamental constants, and relativistic geodesy follows from the same capability. As an instrument builder I judge that this is a tool that changes what can be measured, which fits the statutory category of an invention that has benefited physics. The two-name credit also fits comfortably under the three-person limit, which is not true of B029 or B039.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation remains the novelty margin over the 2005 prize (combs and laser precision spectroscopy) and the 2012 prize (control of single quantum systems, including ion clocks). I now think the answer is that lattice clocks solve a different problem: the ion route gets accuracy from one isolated particle, while the lattice route gets stability from a large ensemble by removing the confining-field shift, so the 1e-18 stability regime is reached by a distinct idea and not by a refinement. That is an argument and not a proof, and I could be overrating it. The second reservation is attribution: NIST, PTB, SYRTE and other groups, and the ion-clock line, are outside the two names. The third is that a precision-metrology capability may carry less weight with the wider community than a discovery about nature such as IceCube or Higgs, and the redefinition of the second is still pending.

responses.point: Mehlig names incrementalism relative to frequency combs (2005) and ion control (2012) as the strongest objection, while stating that the redefinition of the second has no bearing on the science.
responses.response: I agree that the redefinition is a timing question and not a scientific one, and I would not make it a precondition. On incrementalism I part company in degree. Combs supply the counting machinery and ion control supplies single-particle clocks, but neither yields the magic-wavelength cancellation or the many-atom interrogation that gives lattice clocks their stability. The weakness in my own answer is that I have not shown this from the record; it rests on my understanding of the physics. I would therefore support a citation that says neutral atoms and magic-wavelength trapping explicitly, so that the novelty is written into the text and the boundary with the earlier prizes is visible.

responses.point: Danielsson now prefers B012 but stresses that B039, the Higgs discovery, remains the most consequential experimental result on the shortlist, with Gianotti, Jenni and Virdee as a pragmatic selection.
responses.response: I agree that the Higgs discovery is the largest single experimental result on the list, and I ranked it second at opening. Our difference is about whether a defensible prize can be written. The pragmatic selection leaves out Della Negra, whose founding role in CMS is comparable to Virdee's, and it treats leadership as authorship. I would rather not ask the committee to carry that uncertainty into a final vote when a cleaner configuration is available. I keep B039 as an alternative, and I would reconsider only if the committee could state a principled basis for the three names that does not depend on counting roles.

responses.point: Olsson raises whether prospective impacts, such as the redefinition of the second, geodesy and variation of constants, should weigh against demonstrated results, and notes that other lattice-clock groups and the ion-clock line are not credited.
responses.response: My answer is to weigh only what is demonstrated. The 1e-18 uncertainty, its reproduction across species and laboratories, and the clock comparisons are demonstrated; geodesy and searches for varying constants are consequences I treat as supporting context, not as part of the case. On credit I accept that the boundary is defensible and not unique. The honest statement is that Katori's proposal and first realisation and Ye's accuracy frontier are the two contributions the committee members describe consistently, but the files do not verify priority, so I would write the citation around the invention and the 1e-18 realisation and not around a first-to-do-it claim.

responses.point: Kroll names Takamoto and other lattice-clock groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST as contributors outside the two credited names, and a possible case for waiting for the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: Takamoto's strontium demonstration is the example that most tests a two-name credit, and I cannot settle it from the record, as Kroll cannot either. Where I come out is that a prize may credit the invention and the decisive realisation without crediting every successful follow-up, since the reproduction by other groups is evidence that the idea works. I do not think waiting improves the case, because the maturity is already there in the performance. I also note that Kroll's own remote link through Hall's laboratory is disclosed and that I see no reason it should change how his support for B012 is weighed.

uncertainties: Priority and the relative roles of Katori and Ye in the magic-wavelength proposal and early realisations rest on recollection and have not been verified from the supplied record.
Whether Takamoto, SYRTE, PTB or NIST contributions require a different allocation of credit than two names.
Whether the lattice-clock step is sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, which is my judgment and not an established fact.
Whether the committee should treat the pending redefinition of the second as irrelevant, as I do, or as a reason to wait.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B012, Katori or Ye. For disclosure, my work in cosmic-ray, gamma-ray and neutrino-adjacent astroparticle instrumentation and in large collaborations (PAMELA, Fermi-LAT, PoGO, XL-Calibur) makes me close to the field of B029 and the collaboration-credit issue in B039, although the profile records no direct tie to IceCube, ATLAS or CMS or to any credited person. As chair I have counted only positions stated in the round-1 files. Unchanged from round 1.
